“I beg permission to remark, Sir Walter,” said Mr Shepherd one morning at Kellynch Hall, putting down his newspaper, “that the circumstances of the moment are greatly to our advantage. Peace will bring all our wealthy naval officers back to land. They will each be looking for a home. No better season, Sir Walter, for a selection of tenants, and thoroughly responsible ones. Handsome fortunes have been accumulated in the war. Should some prosperous admiral happen to present himself, Sir Walter—”

“He would count himself exceedingly fortunate, Shepherd,” Sir Walter answered; “that is my sole observation. What a prize Kellynch Hall would prove to him! Indeed, the finest of his prizes, however many he may already have captured; eh, Shepherd?”

Mr Shepherd bestowed the laugh he knew this pleasantry demanded, and proceeded—

“I venture to remark, Sir Walter, that naval gentlemen are agreeable people in business transactions. I know something of their manner of conducting affairs, and readily acknowledge that their ideas are exceedingly liberal. They are as likely to prove satisfactory tenants as any class one could encounter. Consequently, Sir Walter, the suggestion I would respectfully offer is this: should any report of your intentions circulate, a possibility we are obliged to consider, knowing how hard it is to hide the proceedings and purposes of one portion of society from the attention and inquisitiveness of another—distinction carries its penalties; I, John Shepherd, could keep whatever domestic concerns I pleased to myself, as nobody would deem me worth observing, but Sir Walter Elliot is watched by eyes he may find it difficult to escape—therefore I will venture so far as to say that, despite every precaution, it would scarcely astonish me if some whisper of the truth were spread. On that assumption, as I meant to observe, applications must certainly ensue, and I should consider those of our rich naval commanders especially deserving of consideration. Let me add that I can come over within two hours at any time, and spare you the inconvenience of answering.”

Sir Walter merely inclined his head. Shortly afterwards, however, he rose, walked about the room, and remarked with sarcasm—

“Few naval gentlemen, I should suppose, would not feel astonished to discover themselves occupying a residence of this sort.”

“They would certainly survey their surroundings and congratulate themselves upon their luck,” said Mrs Clay, who was also there. Her father had brought her in his carriage, since nothing benefited Mrs Clay’s health quite like a drive to Kellynch. “But I entirely share my father’s opinion that a sailor could make a most desirable tenant.

Nightingales lived among the surrounding oaks. I am there again now, with Idris beside me in the lovely first bloom of youth. Remember, I am only twenty-two, and the girl I love has barely lived seventeen summers. Autumn rains have swollen the river until it covers the low ground. Adrian, out in his favourite boat, has chosen the dangerous amusement of gathering the highest branch from a flooded oak. Have you grown tired of living, Adrian, that you play with danger like this?

He has won his prize and steers his boat through the flood. We watch him anxiously, but the current carries him away. He has to land much farther downstream and take a long way round before he can reach us. “He’s safe!” Idris says as he jumps ashore, waving the branch above his head to show his success. “We’ll wait for him here.”

We were alone together. The sun had gone down, and the nightingales began to sing. The evening star shone clearly through the light still lingering in the western sky. My angelic girl’s blue eyes rested on that lovely image of herself. “Look how the light pulses,” she said, “the light that is the star’s life. Its trembling brightness seems to suggest that its existence is as uncertain and changeable as our own on earth. I think it feels fear, and love.”

“Don’t gaze at the star, my dear, generous friend,” I cried. “Don’t find love in its shaking rays, or look at faraway worlds, or speak of a feeling that is only imagined. I have kept silent so long. For so long I have ached to speak to you and offer you my soul, my life, my entire self. Don’t look at the star, my love—or look, and let that eternal spark speak for me. Let its silent shining bear witness and plead my case. Love sustains me as light sustains that star. For as long as its light escapes destruction, I will go on loving you.”

The joy of that moment must remain forever hidden from the world’s unfeeling gaze. I still feel her graceful body against my overflowing heart. Even now the memory of that first kiss makes my sight blur, my pulse falter, and my breath fail. Slowly and without speaking, we went to meet Adrian, whose approach we could hear.

I begged Adrian to come back after taking his sister home. That evening, as we walked the moonlit forest paths, I opened my whole heart to my friend, with all its delight and hope. For a moment he looked troubled. “I should have seen this coming,” he said. “What conflict there will be now!

What sort of existence could they share while Fate continued to weigh this dreadful destiny in her balance? At whatever cost, the wedding must be deferred. On that point his determination was absolute. Though he loved the girl fervently, though the lightest contact with her fingers as they sat side by side sent delicious happiness thrilling through every nerve, he saw his duty no less plainly. He understood entirely that he possessed no right to marry before accomplishing the murder. Once it was done, he might stand at the altar beside Sybil Merton and entrust his life to her without fear of misconduct. Once it was done, he could fold her in his arms, certain that she would never blush on his account or bow her head for shame. But first it had to be accomplished, and the sooner it was, the better for them both.

Many men similarly situated would have chosen the flower-strewn road of pleasure over duty’s arduous heights. Lord Arthur, however, was too scrupulous to place enjoyment before principle. His love contained something beyond simple passion; to him Sybil represented everything noble and good. For an instant he felt a natural revulsion at the deed required of him, but the feeling quickly vanished. His heart assured him that this was sacrifice rather than sin, while reason pointed out that no alternative remained. The choice lay between an existence devoted to himself and one devoted to others. Undeniably appalling though his appointed task might be, he knew he must never let selfishness conquer love. All of us must eventually confront this same decision; the same question comes to everyone. For Lord Arthur it arrived early, before the calculating cynicism of middle age had corrupted his character, or the shallow fashionable selfishness of the present day had eaten into his heart. He therefore felt no reluctance to fulfil his duty. Happily for him, too, he was neither a mere visionary nor a lounging dilettante. Such a man would have faltered like Hamlet, allowing indecision to spoil his intention. Lord Arthur was, at bottom, practical. To him life signified action more than reflection. He possessed the rarest quality of all, common sense.

By now the previous night’s turbulent, disordered emotions had wholly subsided. He remembered his frantic roaming from one street to another and his violent anguish with something approaching embarrassment. Precisely because his suffering had been so sincere, it now seemed scarcely real. He marvelled that he could have behaved so foolishly as to rage and declaim against what could not be avoided.
